body.text: A rout of AI related stocks dragged Wall Street down on Friday, while another rise in oil prices and the massive theft from the world's biggest crypto exchange, Binance, didn't help sentiment.
Westpac has reported a $6.8 billion full year profit as the ASX remains on edge this morning, priced for a flat opening ahead of the RBA rates decision.
Follow the day's financial news and insights from our specialist business reporters on our live blog.
Disclaimer: this blog is not intended as investment advice.

Firmus wins approval for a data centre in Tasmania's north-west
Latrobe Council staff have approved a proposal from AI infrastructure company Firmus Technologies for a research and development facility in Tasmania's north-west.
Firmus wants to develop a 26-megawatt AI data centre and a 26-megawatt R&D facility at the old paper mill site in Wesley Vale.
Latrobe Council has asked the state government to assess the main data centre as a major project, but it has now approved the R&D facility.
The facility is considered a permitted development, meaning it's not required to be publicly advertised or voted on by councillors.
Firmus says an existing warehouse on the site will be repurposed for the facility, which will explore how technology such as batteries can reduce reliance on backup diesel generators.
The company is also building an AI data centre in Launceston and has approval for another at Long Reach in Tasmania's north.
Firmus pulled its highly anticipated initial public offering last month due to lacklustre demand from investors.
Inflation gauge rises in October
Not that the RBA needs much more persuading, but the private sector measure inflation, the Melbourne Institute's Inflation Gauge rose 0.5% in October.
That follows a 0.3% in September, marking the fourth consecutive month of gains.
IFM Investors chief economist Alex Joiner described the result as "ugly".
Dwelling approvals bounce back
Dwelling approvals rose by 5.1%, spurred on by a jump in apartment approvals while house approval slipped in September.
Apartment approvals are notoriously volatile in the ABS series.
They rose 16.6% in September after a 21.7% fall in August, in seasonally adjusted terms.
House approvals fell 5.3% to 10,432 dwellings, following a 5.4% rise in August.
ABS head of construction statistics, Daniel Rossi said the September fall in private sector house approvals is the largest since August 2025.
"Despite this drop, it is the ninth consecutive month where more than 10,000 private sector houses have been approved across Australia," Mr Rossi noted.
ASX slips ahead of RBA decision, banks boosted by Westpac, miners dumped
The ASX has opened lower, with demand for the banks being offset by a slump in the mining sector.
At 11:20am (AEDT) the ASX 200 was down 0.2% to 8,892 points.

Ahead of tomorrow's RBA interest decision, and the expected 25bp hike, retailers are split with consumer cyclicals (discretionary) making gains and consumer non-cyclicals (non-discretionary) on the slide.
The discretionary side of things is being led by Tabcorp (+2.3%), with investors having a punt on it ahead of the Melbourne Cup tomorrow.

On the non-discretionary side of the aisle, the supermarkets are still suffering from last week's poor sales numbers from Coles (-2.7%). The blog commends the ASX for nominating alcohol retailer Endeavour (-0.6%) as non-discretionary retail.
The Big Four banks are all stronger after Westpac's results. Westpac is leading the way (+1.5%) despite some concern around shrinking margins.
The real estate sector, which is also interest rate sensitive, is doing well. GPT is up 2.4%.
However, it is the broad church of the industrial sector that is leading the way. Plumbing supplier Reece is up more than 5% on broker upgrades.
On the other hand, miners are being sold on the back of softer commodity prices on Friday. Rio Tinto has shed 1.4%.
Despite the spot price edging up this morning, gold stocks are out of favour as the spot price hovers near a one-year low. Newmont and Northern Star are both down more than 3%.
Health care is patchy. Resmed (-7.0%) is still suffering from a poorly received earnings update.
The good news story is CSL (+0.5%) has nudged back above $200/share mark for the first time in a year, a more than 100% gain on its low point in May.
The top mover on the ASX 200 is Reece, while titanium miner IperionX (+4.7%) is doing well too.
The bottom mover is gold miner Catalist Metals (-10%).
Key Event
Westpac gains on result
Westpac has outperformed its "Big Four" retail bank peers this morning after posting its FY2026 results.
At 10:30am (AEDT), Westpac had gained 0.9% in a generally positive start for the banks this morning.
Only NAB, which reports on Thursday, has lost ground, and that is only marginal (-0.05%).

Key Event
Westpac faces downgrades after 'soft' result: JP Morgan
The first review of Westpac's FY26 $6.8 billion profit is in, and it isn't a 5-star, standing applause sort of take.

JP Morgan's veteran bank analyst Andrew Triggs says the result was softer than expected, with a "0.7% miss at NPAT (net profit after tax) level ex notable items, driven by weakness in core NIM (net interest margin)".
Mr Triggs said revenue was a 0.5% miss compared to JP Morgan's estimate, while expenses were 0.4% better.
"Core NIM was very weak in 4Q26, and will likely be the focus of the conference call and driver of small EPS (earnings per share) downgrades," he said.
"Lending pressure was attributed to Australian and NZ mortgages."
Mr Triggs was also concerned by Westpac's weaker overall revenue trends.
He identified the bank's strong capital levels and credit quality as key positives, along with solid guidance on costs and an "in-line" dividend payout.
Key Event
Manufacturing contraction continues
Activity in Australia's factories has contracted for the second consecutive month, according to S&P Global's latest Purchasing Managers' Index (PMI) survey.
S&P Global noted a sharper fall in new orders drove another solid decline in output.
"In turn, goods producers scaled back both their purchasing activity and employment and also cut back on their inventory holdings as demand deteriorated," S&P Global said.

While the decline to 49.6 points represents only a marginal decline in activity — 50 points is the break-even point between expansion and contraction — the October PMI reading was the joint lowest since December 2024.
S&P Global economist Jingyi Pan said the survey showed manufacturers faced a "double whammy" at the start of the fourth quarter, with supply constraints piling on top of worsening demand.

"Subdued market conditions, higher interest rates and elevated prices contributed to the sharpest drop in new orders in almost two years, while shipment delays and port congestions were causes for one of the steepest extensions of delivery times since the post-COVID-19 pandemic period," she said.

"It was positive, however, to see business confidence recovering slightly from the September low amid hopes for improvements in the coming months. That said, the level of overall business optimism remained subdued by historical standards."
Key Event
NT data centre scraps start date on EPA concerns

The developer of one of Australia's biggest planned data centres has scrapped its target start date after a regulator said it needed longer than usual to set environmental parameters, a setback to the country's ambitions to be a fast-track destination for AI investment.

Startup Energy North, which says it has finance lined up for a sprawling gas and solar-powered data centre on a cattle ranch 100 kilometres south of Daly Waters (680km south of Darwin), had given a "first power" date of June 28, 2028, in regulatory filings four months ago.

But after the Northern Territory environment regulator said in an October 7 ruling it was suspending its seven-week deadline to decide what hurdles the project must clear, the developer told Reuters it had scrubbed its timeline.

"The June 2028 date in our referral was an indicative schedule at the time of lodgement, and we're no longer working to it," said Energy North vice-president of project development Daniel Hunter in an email.

The project is the biggest in Australia to put back its timing and shows how data centre ambitions face hurdles even in the isolated north, which has sought to differentiate itself from cities in the contest for the $7 trillion McKinsey forecasts will be invested in "AI factories" globally by 2030.

The Territory is counting on luring projects with its vast supply of uninhabited land and sunshine — 260,000 residents in an area twice the size of Texas, with as much sun as the Sahara — and a huge just-opened shale gas reserve for backup power.

But stopping the clock on Energy North, the Territory's regulator said it would seek advice from the federal government, which is "developing policy expectations for data centres and AI infrastructure developers", and gave no new timeframe.

Mr Hunter said the project was unfazed and would confirm timing once the regulator sets out terms for an environmental impact statement, required to identify and address potential adverse effects. He declined to say who is lined up to finance the project.
Reuters
Wall Street anxiety mounts despite strong earnings growth
Halfway through Wall Street Q3 reporting season, earnings are coming in better than expected, but that has not stopped conniptions like last Friday's sell-off occurring.
On JP Morgan's calculations, more than 80% of S&P 500 companies that have reported beat EPS (earnings per share) estimates.
The big investment bank's equity strategy team says EPS growth for these companies is at +19% y/y, which beats estimates by more than 3 percentage points.
"All sectors are positively contributing to aggregate EPS growth, with tech, industrials and energy the biggest drivers," JP Morgan wrote in a note to clients over the weekend.
But still investors are worried, and this week another wall of worry confronts them.
The quarterly results so far have intensified concerns about financing and financial returns needed to support the AI investment theme at the heart of the US bull stock market.
The questions are likely to persist, with Apple, AMD, Qualcomm and Palantir among the major tech and AI players due to report next week.
Also, the midterm elections could determine the outlook for AI regulation.
Tuesday's elections will determine whether Democrats can wrest control of Congress away from President Donald Trump's Republican party.

Democrats are widely predicted to win the House of Representatives, but the Senate is more in doubt. Republicans controlled both chambers of Congress during the first two years of the Trump administration.
Investors are bracing for increasing pushback on data centres, whose impact on energy costs and the environment has led to intense public opposition.
Despite doubts that any viable legislation will pose serious risks to AI investment, regardless of which party wins, a Democratic sweep is expected to bring more scrutiny.
Defence and health care are other stock market areas that could be sensitive to the election results.

Any shift in Washington could affect the outlook for fiscal spending that could reverberate through asset prices. A Democratic sweep could bring more regulatory scrutiny, including for Wall Street banks and crypto firms.
With Reuters
Home prices to fall 15% top-to-bottom: AMP
Depending on one's perspective, national average home prices fell another 1.2%, or housing affordability improved marginally across October.
The move was sufficient to have AMP chief economist Shane Oliver revise his thinking this morning on the extent of the fall over the cycle.
"We now expect a 15% top to bottom fall, revised from a 10–15% fall," Dr Oliver said.
"The pace of decline is now tracking the fastest in the period since 1980 with national average prices down 6.7% and capital city average prices now down 8.1% from their highs early this year.

"The rapid decline, more rate hikes than expected and rising unemployment combined with the structural change associated with the tax hikes on investors suggest that the top to bottom fall is now likely to be around 15%."
To read more, check out the very excellent Nassim Khadem's very excellent report on the October data.
Key Event
Westpac CEO says economy is holding up 'relatively well'
Westpac CEO Anthony Miller says the Australian economy is holding up "relatively well" in a time of global uncertainty.

"Strong business investment [is] supporting the medium-term outlook. This is evident across our Business and Institutional customer base where demand for credit remain strong," Mr Miller said while releasing the bank's 2026 FY results.
"However, inflation remains above the Reserve Bank's target range and interest rates are likely to remain elevated into 2027.
"This is presenting challenges for many households and businesses, although the impacts are uneven across the country."
Westpac's margins narrow
Westpac has seen its net interest margins narrow, down 7bps to 1.87%.
This is marginally below analyst expectations of the NIM coming in at 1.89%.
The net interest margin is the difference between what the bank pays for deposits and the rate it lends at; a key measure of profitability to 9.85%
The bank's return on average ordinary equity slipped 6bps to 9.6%.

Its capital stocks were also lower, despite the sale of the RAMS home loans business. The CET1 capital ratio (the top tier measure of a bank's capital) was down 7 bps to 12.5%, but this was about $2.9 billion above the bank's target of 11.25%
Westpac says credit quality is 'resilient'
Westpac has reported a decline in the value of its stressed loans.
Stressed exposures as a percentage of Tangible Common Equity (TCE) declined 11bps to 1.17% as of September, the bank said.
Over the year, credit impairment provisions increased by $5.2 billion and the ratio of collectively assessed provisions to credit RWA (risk weighted assets) was higher at 127 basis points.
Key Event
Binance hit by customer withdrawals after returning to trade
First, it was the thieves, then the customers moved in to shrink the assets of the world's biggest crypto exchange Binance.

Having just resumed trading after hackers made off with $US6.3 billion in what's being called the biggest bank heist in history, customers moved with the speed of the hackers themselves to shovel another $US3.6 billion ($5.1 billion) out the door.
That (legal) withdrawal represents more than 2% of Binance's assets.
However, that may be understating things. Crypto analytics platform DefiLlama said on its dashboard that outflows were higher, at $US4.4 billion ($6.3 billion).
Binance said withdrawals were stabilising after an initial spike and deposit volumes had remained "substantial". The exchange said it had now covered 95% of the $6.3 billion of stolen assets.
As Reuters reports, the heist, which analysts believe may be the biggest financial robbery ever, adds to a string of recent crypto thefts.

Withdrawal levels are an early test of whether customers still trust the exchange with their money after the attack.Attackers stole $US2.9 billion ($4.1 billion) worth of cryptocurrency across nearly 150 incidents last year, according to researchers at TRM Labs.

Big tech's really bad month
A trillion here, a trillion there — and pretty soon you're talking serious money.
Indeed, more than $US2.6 trillion ($3.7 trillion) was wiped off the market value of the big tech stocks last month.
The Nasdaq shed about 6% as the AI trade ran into turbulence, with hyperscalers Meta Platforms, Alphabet and Amazon raising spending forecasts further as they race to expand AI infrastructure.
Alphabet suffered its biggest one-day percentage drop on record on Thursday after disappointing results in the core business of search advertising and a massive acceleration in cash burn.

Meta's plans for a record $US97.5 billion fund raise heightened concerns about shareholder dilution and whether mounting AI spending could force other Big Tech companies to increasingly tap capital markets.
Independent global investment strategist Gerard Minack says the investment bear case for AI is simple.
"The profits on selling AI services will generate a lousy return on the invested capital," Mr Minack wrote in a note to clients last week.
"History shows big investment booms end in a bust.
"Less dramatically, it also shows that companies that grow assets fast almost always underperform.
"There are no signs that AI providers will build the barriers to entry required to generate super-normal profits.
"Timing when the boom busts is fraught but AI stocks are no longer outperforming the market.
"History is unequivocal: big capex booms never end well for the original investors," Mr Minack said.
With Reuters
Key Event
Westpac reports $6.8 billion full year profit
Westpac has reported a $6.8 billion net profit for the full year, 2026.
Its cash profit, excluding one-off items, came in at $7.0 billion, slightly above the consensus figure of $6.96 billion calculated by analysts.
The full year dividend came in at $1.54 per share, 1% higher than FY25.

The RBA rates decision on Tuesday is the big event for the week.

There's not much point previewing it, the subject has been thrashed to death from pillar to post; that is everyone from the economists at the four big pillar banks down to the humblest blog post … and there's been furious agreement that inflation is too high and the RBA board will raise the cash rate by 25bps to 4.85%. (They said that about the RBNZ last week too, but that's a different story we suppose.)
The more important issue may well be the post-decision communication from the board and the governor's post-decision media conference.

The other releases of note locally include the always-volatile dwelling approvals (later this morning), the ABS Household Spending Indicator (Wednesday), which while being flat month-on-month has a strong annual growth of 6.8% and international trade (Thursday) which may swing into deficit due to a sharp increase in the price of refined fuel imports in September.

This week also marks to start of the big banks' mini reporting season — that is, for banks not named the "Commonwealth Bank of Australia", which marches to a different beat and released its $11 billion full year profit in August.
Westpac kicks things off this morning, followed by NAB on Thursday and Macquarie posts its half year numbers on Friday.
ANZ will give the blog something to mull over next Monday, November 9.
Offshore, the big events are very much US-centric … mid-term elections (Wednesday) and the key jobs numbers of non-farm payrolls and unemployment on Friday.
The Bank of England meets on Thursday and is tipped to raise rates by 25bps to 4.0%.
Key Event
Wall Street tumbles on mounting AI fears, ASX on edge
Wall Street closed the week, maybe not in a blind panic, but there was certainly a disquieting dumping of stocks as investors fled to the exits and the weekend.
All three key indices fell sharply, the tech-centric Nasdaq fell the hardest and is down almost 8% from its record high of just three weeks ago.
• Nasdaq: 2.9%
The dump saw the global MSCI down 1.5% for the day, while the pan-continental Eurostoxx 600 fell a comparatively modest 0.4%.
The tech-lite ASX is unlikely to be as affected by anxieties over cash-burning AI investments as Wall Street was on Friday.
When trading closed on Saturday morning (AEDT) ASX 200 futures were flat, or to be precise 4 points (0.04%) lower.
The tech rout was sparked by disappointing quarterly results from Intel and Amazon released late on Thursday.
While Amazon pared losses as the session progressed, Intel shares cratered, down almost 30%.
Chip stocks veered sharply lower, with Nvidia down more than 4%.
The broader chips index shed 7.2%, slumping to a monthly loss of more than 15%. Server makers Dell and HP dropped 10.8% and 9.6%, respectively.

"It's fair to say that this week, not just today, has been very much about the future of AI and what that's going to look like, whether there will be a positive return on investment and if so, how quickly," Wealthspire adviser Oliver Pursche told Reuters.
"Companies that are performing and meeting the very lofty expectations that have been set are doing well," Mr Pursche said.
"Those that are falling short and seem to be missing the mark or not executing as expected are getting punished."

On the subject of being punished, cryptocurrency related firms all got walloped on the news that hackers nicked a lazy $US6.3 billion ($9 billion) worth of various stable coins, such as Bitcoin and Ethereum, while no-one was looking at the world's biggest crypto exchange Binance.
Listed crypto firms Coinbase, Strategy and Robin Hood all fell between 7 and 11%. All said they were safe, but they would say that.
Putting aside the Binance contretemps, it's worth noting that hackers have made off with about $US3 billion in crypto in around 150 incidents.
US Treasuries were one of the beneficiaries of the tech rout as investors decided they were a safer bet at the moment, which is saying something.
The benchmark 10-year yield closed the month with its biggest monthly drop in nearly three years.

Gold, once also considered a safe haven, didn't benefit from the conniptions — indeed, it slumped (-3.5%) to a one-year low, along with other precious metals. Silver shed 6.5% and palladium shed 3.0%.

"The sky is falling," independent metals trader Tai Wong told Reuters with a dramatic flourish."Metals will not be able to escape the gravity well of a nasty stock correction. Earnings have been the foundation of the AI rally and now that pillar is showing some cracks."

Oil seems to be blithely ignoring Mr Wong's "gravity well". The key benchmarks both gained more than 2% on Friday.
• Brent crude futures: +2.4% to $US117.64/barrel
• WTI crude futures: +2.1% to $US113.43/barrel
For the month, Brent finished almost 14% higher, while WTI rose even more, up 15%.
On Friday, a tanker in the Strait of Hormuz was hit by explosive devices, believed to be limpet mines attached by a small boat, according to UKMTO, the British maritime security service.
It is believed to be the first successful use of limpet mines since the war began in February. Probably not the last either.

Good morning
Good morning and welcome to another day on the ABC markets and finance blog.
Stephen Letts from ABC business team limbering up for a blow-by-blow coverage of the day's events, where every post is hopefully a winner, but none should be construed as financial advice.
Wall Street closed sharply lower on Friday, driven down a major sell-off of AI-related stocks.
The ASX, largely an AI-free zone, is poised to open flat, with futures trading pointing to only a marginal loss ahead of tomorrow's RBA rates decision.
It's a busy day ahead.
We've already seen October's home price numbers — a nationwide decline of 1.2%.

We'll have more housing news a bit later with September's dwelling approvals being released and Westpac's full year results will be posted very soon — and they are likely to be a key driver of sentiment today.
The key number to look out for is a cash profit of $6.96 billion. That's the consensus forecast among the analysts.
The game's afoot, so let's get blogging.
